fact: At NOAA's Fort Collins station an average year has 150 nights at or below 32°F, only 15.4 of them on days that never rise above 32°F (so about 135 days freeze and then warm above freezing), 4.4 nights at or below 0°F, 43.6 days with an inch or more of snow on the ground, and a median last spring freeze of May 2 (1991–2020 normals).
quote: USC00053005 FT COLLINS — ANN-TMIN-AVGNDS-LSTH032 150.0 · ANN-TMAX-AVGNDS-LSTH032 15.4 · ANN-TMIN-AVGNDS-LSTH000 4.4 · ANN-SNWD-AVGNDS-GE001WI 43.6 · ANN-TMIN-PRBLST-T32FP50 05/02 · ANN-TMIN-PRBFST-T32FP50 10/07 · MAM-SNOW-NORMAL 17.2 · ANN-SNOW-NORMAL 51.4
source_label: NOAA NCEI U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020, annual/seasonal, station FT COLLINS (USC00053005): freeze and snow elements
notes: Element definitions from NOAA's Normals_ANN_Documentation_1991-2020.pdf: LSTH032 (TMIN) = days with minimum <= 32F; LSTH032 (TMAX) = days with maximum <= 32F; LSTH000 = days with minimum <= 0F; SNWD GE001WI = days with snow depth >= 1 inch; PRBLST/PRBFST T32FP50 = 50% probability date of last spring / first fall 32F. The 'about 135' freeze-then-thaw days is our arithmetic (150.0 − 15.4 = 134.6: days with a low at or below 32F and a high above it), not a NOAA element. MAM snow = March–May. Station-to-town assignment by proximity (INFERENCE) — say 'the nearest NOAA station'.

fact: At NOAA's Loveland 2N station an average year has 173.9 nights at or below 32°F, only 19.9 of them on days that never rise above 32°F (so about 154 days freeze and then warm above freezing), 9.6 nights at or below 0°F, 49.0 days with an inch or more of snow on the ground, and a median last spring freeze of May 10 (1991–2020 normals).
quote: USC00055236 LOVELAND 2N — ANN-TMIN-AVGNDS-LSTH032 173.9 · ANN-TMAX-AVGNDS-LSTH032 19.9 · ANN-TMIN-AVGNDS-LSTH000 9.6 · ANN-SNWD-AVGNDS-GE001WI 49.0 · ANN-TMIN-PRBLST-T32FP50 05/10 · ANN-TMIN-PRBFST-T32FP50 10/01 · MAM-SNOW-NORMAL 14.7 · ANN-SNOW-NORMAL 47.0

fact: At NOAA's Longmont 2 ESE station an average year has 177.7 nights (about 178) at or below 32°F, only 18.5 of them on days that never rise above 32°F (so about 159 days freeze and then warm above freezing), 8.4 nights at or below 0°F, and a median last spring freeze of May 7 (1991–2020 normals).
quote: USC00055116 LONGMONT 2 ESE — ANN-TMIN-AVGNDS-LSTH032 177.7 · ANN-TMAX-AVGNDS-LSTH032 18.5 · ANN-TMIN-AVGNDS-LSTH000 8.4 · ANN-TMIN-PRBLST-T32FP50 05/07 · ANN-TMIN-PRBFST-T32FP50 10/05

fact: The Colorado Climate Center says chinook winds on the high plains bring large, sudden temperature rises, and rises of 25 to 35°F within a short time are not uncommon.
quote: Warmed by rapid descent from higher levels, these winds bring large and sudden temperature rises. This phenomenon is the "chinook;" of the high plains and temperature rises of 25 to 35°F within a short time are not uncommon.
source_label: Colorado Climate Center (Colorado State University), Climate of Colorado
notes: The page renders the degree sign as the HTML entity &degF. The same page says chinooks 'greatly moderate average winter temperatures in areas near enough to the mountains to experience them frequently'. Do not quote the page's comparison sentence that names an out-of-state place.

fact: The Colorado Climate Center says snow cover acts as an insulating blanket that can protect soils from deep freezes on extremely cold days.
quote: Snow can act as an insulating "blanket". Even though we associate snow with cold, on extremely cold days, snow cover can actually protect soils from deep freezes.
source_label: Colorado Climate Center (Colorado State University), Snow in Colorado

fact: Larimer County's building department sets a minimum frost depth of 30 inches below grade countywide for footings.
quote: 1809.5 Frost protection. Minimum frost depth is 30 inches below grade countywide.
source_label: Larimer County Community Development, Structural Design Information (2024 IRC/IBC, updated January 2026)
notes: curl gets a Cloudflare 403 challenge; the PDF was read through a fetch tool and converted with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. It is a design value for building footings in the county's building jurisdiction, not a measured freeze depth for any one yard. Say 'designs footings for frost 30 inches down', never 'the ground freezes 30 inches every winter'.

fact: Weld County's building department uses a frost line depth of 30 inches in its design criteria for residential and commercial structures in unincorporated Weld County.
quote: Climatic and Geographical Design Criteria for Residential Structures 2024 IRC … Frost Line Depth … 30”
source_label: Weld County Building Department, Design Criteria and Adopted Building Codes (2024 codes, effective June 15, 2026)
notes: The criteria are a table; the quote joins the table title, the column header and the value with ellipses. curl gets a 403; the PDF was read through a fetch tool and converted with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. The same table gives an air freezing index of 1224 and a winter design temperature of 1. Applies to unincorporated Weld County; towns run their own building departments. A design value for footings, not a measured freeze depth.

fact: Frost heave needs three things at once, a frost-susceptible soil with a significant amount of fine particles, freezing temperatures that reach into the soil, and water, while clean sands and gravels with few fines are not frost susceptible.
quote: The three elements necessary for ice lenses and thus frost heave are: Frost susceptible soil (significant amount of fines). Subfreezing temperatures (freezing temperatures must penetrate the soil and, in general, the thickness of an ice lens will be thicker with slower rates of freezing). Water (must be available from the groundwater table, infiltration, an aquifer, or held within the voids of fine-grained soil). … This problem occurs primarily in soils containing fine particles (often termed “frost susceptible” soils), while clean sands and gravels (small amounts of fine particles) are non-frost susceptible (NFS).
source_label: Pavement Interactive (Pavement Tools Consortium), Frost Action
notes: Pavement engineering reference; the same page says many agencies classify material as frost susceptible when 10 percent or more passes a No. 200 sieve. The page is about pavements; the page applies the principle to a turf base and the soil under it.

fact: In a sudden thaw the ground melts from the surface down, and the still-frozen soil underneath traps the meltwater so it can only drain sideways or across the surface.
quote: During a sudden spring thaw, melting will proceed almost entirely from the surface downward. This type of thawing leads to extremely poor drainage conditions. The frozen soil beneath the thawed layer can trap the water released by the melting ice lenses so that lateral and surface drainage are the only paths the water can take.
source_label: Pavement Interactive (Pavement Tools Consortium), Frost Action

fact: FieldTurf, a synthetic sports-turf maker, says the components of its turf system do not freeze but the moisture in the infill does.
quote: while the components of your FieldTurf system do not freeze, moisture within the infill does. This frozen moisture allows you to plow the field safely without displacing a meaningful amount of infill.
source_label: FieldTurf, Everything You Need to Know About Snow Removal
notes: Written for sports fields. The plowing advice belongs to the snow-removal guide; this page uses only the freezing statement.

fact: SIS Pitches, a synthetic sports-surface builder, says snow and ice are not harmful to synthetic grass and should generally be left to melt and drain off on their own.
quote: Snow and ice are not harmful to synthetic grass pitches and generally should be left to melt and drain off the system without assistance.
source_label: SIS Pitches, Winter maintenance advice for synthetic pitches

fact: SIS Pitches says frozen synthetic grass can be played on if the footing is adequate, but heavy use should be discouraged because the fibre is relatively brittle at low temperatures and shock absorption is substantially reduced.
quote: Provided that the foothold is adequate, the pitch may be played on when frozen, but heavy use is to be discouraged because the fibre is relatively brittle at low temperatures. The degree of shock absorption will also be substantially reduced and players should be made aware of this fact.
source_label: SIS Pitches, Winter maintenance advice for synthetic pitches

fact: SIS Pitches says rain or a quick thaw on frozen synthetic grass can flood it because the sand infill is still frozen and stops water draining, and it drains normally once the infill thaws.
quote: If heavy rain falls on a frozen pitch, or the snow and ice thaw quickly, the field may become flooded. This is because the sand in the infill is still frozen and prevents the water draining. This is not a problem, as the field will drain properly once the infill has thawed.
source_label: SIS Pitches, Winter maintenance advice for synthetic pitches

fact: CSU Extension says heavy, wet snows in late spring or early autumn are common in Colorado.
quote: In Colorado, heavy, wet snows in the late spring or early autumn are common.
source_label: CSU Extension, Colorado Gardening: Challenge to Newcomers (reviewed November 2025)
